title: The Story of the Blind Man Baba Abdullah (简体中文)
summary: The blind beggar of the bridge was brought before Caliph Harun al-Rashid, kneeling humbly upon the carpet of audience. [ZH]
keywords: the story of the blind man baba abdullah
full_text:
The blind beggar of the bridge was brought before Caliph Harun al-Rashid, kneeling humbly upon the carpet of audience.

'O Commander of the Faithful,' Baba Abdullah began, 'my sightlessness was not born of disease, but carved out by the poisonous thorn of boundless greed.

In my youth, I was an enterprising camel merchant, owning eighty sturdy beasts. One day, returning from Basra with empty pack-saddles, I encountered an ascetic dervish resting near an oasis. In conversation, he told me of a hidden valley among the desolate mountains containing treasure beyond the dreams of kings. He offered to lead me there on condition that we split the gold evenly, forty camel-loads for him and forty for me.

I gladly swore solemn oaths. We rode into a narrow canyon where the dervish kindled a fragrant fire and threw herbs into the smoke. The earth cleft asunder, revealing a subterranean vault filled with gold chalices, pearls, and diamonds.

We loaded all eighty camels until they knelt under the glorious weight. As we parted at the crossroads, jealousy ignited within my soul. I thought: "He is a monk with no family; what need has he of forty camels?" I rode after him, pleading that handling forty beasts would distract his devotions. He smilingly surrendered ten, then twenty, until at last, through shameless badgering, I coaxed all eighty back into my possession!

Still unsatisfied, I noticed a tiny golden box in his sash. "What is that?" I asked.
"It holds a magical salve," replied the dervish. "If anointed upon the left eye, it reveals all hidden treasures buried in the earth. But beware: if applied to the right eye, blindness follows instantly."

I begged him to test it on my left eye. He did so, and immediately the soil beneath my feet appeared like transparent crystal, showing veins of gold, forgotten vaults, and sunken emeralds!

A demonic covetousness seized my reason. I reasoned: "If the left eye sees treasures beneath the earth, surely the right eye will reveal the treasures of heaven and jinn!" Despite his solemn warnings, I demanded he anoint my right eye.

He touched my right eyelid. Instantly, an impenetrable pitch-black darkness enveloped me forever! The golden visions vanished. When I cried out in terror and groveled for help, the dervish mounted the lead camel and rode away, saying:
"Thou hadst wealth enough for twenty lifetimes, Baba Abdullah, but thy greed could not endure a single empty corner in thy heart."

I was left alone in the wilderness until wandering shepherds rescued me. In bitter penitence, I vowed that every coin given to me must be accompanied by a stroke upon my cheek, to remind my soul of the foolish greed that traded eternal sight for dirt.'

Harun al-Rashid sighed with profound sadness and decreed:
'Thy punishment was severe, Baba Abdullah, but thy repentance is sincere. Henceforth, receive a daily pension from our treasury, and cease asking blows from strangers, for thou hast borne thy lesson to the core.'
moral: Greed blinds the spiritual eye long before it takes away physical sight; contentment is the true cure for desire. [ZH]
